items.stem: A company runs a photo-sharing website. Users upload photos to an Amazon S3 bucket at sporadic times: some days bring a few photos, and some hours bring hundreds. Each photo needs a thumbnail, and creating one takes a few seconds. The company wants each thumbnail to be ready soon after its photo arrives. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Run a cron job on an Amazon EC2 instance that lists the bucket every minute and creates thumbnails for the new photos.
options.why: It works, but [polling can be highly inefficient](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-eda-polling-inefficient), and the team runs, patches and monitors the instance and the job.

options.text: Configure an S3 event notification that invokes an AWS Lambda function, and create the thumbnail in the function for each new photo.
options.why: Lambda suits [event-driven tasks, unpredictable workloads](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-choose-functions-event-driven-unpredictable), and Amazon S3 invokes the function for each new photo, so nothing waits or polls between uploads.

options.text: Run a container on AWS Fargate all day that polls the bucket for new photos and creates a thumbnail for each one.
options.why: It works, but the container runs and polls between uploads, and with a Lambda function you do not [pay for idle capacity](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-no-pay-for-idle-capacity).
options.misconception: keeps a poller running all day for work that arrives at sporadic times

options.text: Send each upload through a load balancer to an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances that create the thumbnails.
options.why: It works, but the team manages instances, a load balancer and scaling rules for a task that takes a few seconds per photo.

items.explanation: The work starts with an upload, lasts a few seconds and arrives at sporadic times. Amazon S3 is an [event-driven; asynchronous invocation](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-trigger-s3-async) source for Lambda, and with Lambda you [run code without provisioning or managing servers](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-serverless-manages-infrastructure). The event notification replaces any poller, instance or scaling policy.
items.takeaway: Short work that starts when a file arrives fits an S3 event notification that invokes a Lambda function.
items.twin: If the stem said "creating each thumbnail takes about 40 minutes" instead: containers on AWS Fargate, because Fargate has [no hard limit on execution time](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-no-execution-time-limit).
items.say: Each upload fires an S3 event that invokes a Lambda function, so there's no poller and no instance to run.

solvers.stem_only: Use an S3 event notification on object creation that invokes a Lambda function to build each thumbnail; serverless, scales with the bursty uploads, nothing to manage.

items.stem: A company runs an AWS Lambda function that compresses images that users upload. Monitoring shows that the function is CPU-bound: it uses little of its configured memory, but each invocation takes many seconds of computation. The company wants each invocation to finish faster and does not want to change the function code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
keywords: uses little of its configured memory

options.text: Raise the timeout of the function so that each invocation has more time to finish its compression work.
options.why: A longer timeout lets the run last longer, but the timeout [limits the duration of the entire Invoke phase](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-invoke-phase-limited-by-timeout) and adds no compute power.
options.misconception: believes that a longer timeout makes the code run faster

options.text: Keep the memory setting, and choose a larger vCPU setting for the function in its configuration.
options.why: No separate CPU setting exists: Lambda allocates CPU power [in proportion to the amount of memory](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-cpu-proportional-to-memory) that you configure.

options.text: Increase the memory setting of the function so that Lambda allocates more CPU power to the function.
options.why: Lambda allocates CPU power [in proportion to the amount of memory](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-cpu-proportional-to-memory), so a larger memory setting gives the CPU-bound code more compute with no code change.

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency for the function so that its execution environments stay initialized.
options.why: Provisioned concurrency keeps functions ready to respond in [double-digit milliseconds](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-pc-what), which removes start-up delay, not the compute time of each invocation.
options.misconception: believes that initialized environments run the handler code faster

items.explanation: The function is CPU-bound, so it needs more compute power. Lambda allocates CPU power [in proportion to the amount of memory](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-cpu-proportional-to-memory), and for CPU-bound functions [increasing the memory can help resolve the compute](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-memory-tuning-cpu-bound) bottleneck. A larger memory setting is one configuration change, and the code stays the same.
items.takeaway: Raise the memory of a CPU-bound function: Lambda allocates CPU [in proportion to the amount of memory](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-cpu-proportional-to-memory).
items.twin: If the stem said "the first request after a quiet period is slow" instead: provisioned concurrency, because it keeps functions ready to respond in [double-digit milliseconds](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-pc-what).
items.say: Lambda has no CPU knob: you raise memory, and CPU grows with it.

solvers.stem_only: Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to the memory setting, so raise the memory setting; no code change needed.

items.stem: A company runs a serverless order application on AWS Lambda in one AWS Region and keeps a standby copy in a second Region for disaster recovery. Last year, the company requested and received a higher Lambda concurrency quota in the primary Region. During a failover test, many requests to the functions in the standby Region fail with throttling errors. The company must ensure that the standby Region can carry the full production load. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: standby Region fail with throttling errors

options.text: Request the same concurrency quota increase for the standby Region now, and add a check that compares the quotas of both Regions.
options.why: Quotas for concurrent executions apply [per AWS Region](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-quota-scope-region-vs-vpc), and AWS advises a check for a quota [changed in one region but not in other regions](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-wa-quotas-failover-region).

options.text: Make no change, because the quota increase in the primary Region also applies in the standby Region, and the throttling in the test was temporary.
options.why: Quotas for concurrent executions apply [per AWS Region](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-quota-scope-region-vs-vpc), so the increase in the primary Region leaves the standby Region at its own quota.

options.text: Wait for a real failover, and let AWS raise the concurrency quota in the standby Region automatically when the throttling starts.
options.why: [Assuming that quotas will automatically be increased](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-wa-quotas-not-auto-increased) is a known anti-pattern; you [request and track quota increases](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-wa-quotas-not-auto-increased) ahead of the need.

options.text: Run the standby copy of the application on an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 instances instead of on Lambda functions.
options.why: It works, but the team takes on instances, scaling policies and patching for the standby copy, and one quota request fixes the throttling.

items.explanation: The functions in the standby Region are throttled, so that Region lacks concurrency. Quotas for concurrent executions apply [per AWS Region](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-quota-scope-region-vs-vpc), so the increase of last year covers the primary Region alone. One quota request for the standby Region fixes the gap, and an automated check finds any quota [changed in one region but not in other regions](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-wa-quotas-failover-region) later.
items.takeaway: Lambda concurrency quotas apply [per AWS Region](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-quota-scope-region-vs-vpc): raise the quota in the standby Region before a failover needs it.
items.twin: If the stem said "requests to the functions in the primary Region fail with throttling errors during a sales event" instead: request a higher quota in the primary Region, because that Region has reached its own quota.
items.say: Lambda quotas are per Region, so the standby Region needs its own increase before a failover.

solvers.stem_only: Lambda concurrency quotas are per Region; request the same quota increase in the standby Region ahead of time and keep the two Regions' quotas in sync.

items.stem: A company's order service calls an AWS Lambda function synchronously through the AWS SDK and does not use the function's response. Sometimes the function fails because a downstream inventory system is briefly unavailable, and those orders are lost. The company wants to decouple the order service from the function. The company must ensure that failed orders are retried and then kept for review, without changes to the inventory system. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: does not use the function's response
retried and then kept for review

options.text: Keep the synchronous call, and rely on Lambda to retry each failed invocation automatically before it returns an error to the order service.
options.why: Lambda does not retry a synchronous invocation for you: the caller has to [retry the invocation manually](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sync-error-caller-retries), so the failed orders are still lost.

options.text: Keep the synchronous call, and configure a dead-letter queue on the function to keep the orders that fail every attempt.
options.why: An event goes to a [dead letter queue](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-dlq-after-retries) after an asynchronous invocation exhausts its retries, and a synchronous call returns its error to the caller instead.

options.text: Add retry code with backoff to the order service, and write each order that still fails to a database table for review.
options.why: It works, but the team writes and runs retry code and a review table that asynchronous invocation and a destination already provide.

options.text: Invoke the function asynchronously, and configure an on-failure destination that sends the failed events to an Amazon SQS queue.
options.why: Lambda [places the event in a queue](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-async-queue-then-separate-process), retries a failed event [two more times](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-async-default-two-retries), and the destination then keeps a copy for review.

items.explanation: The order service does not need the response, so it can invoke the function asynchronously. Lambda then retries errors, and after the last attempt [Lambda discards it](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-async-discard-then-destination) unless a failed-event destination keeps a copy. The destination can be [a standard SQS queue](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-async-destination-targets), so the team reviews failed orders there.
items.takeaway: A synchronous caller has to [retry the invocation manually](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sync-error-caller-retries); for retries by Lambda, invoke asynchronously with an on-failure destination.
items.twin: If the stem said "needs the function's result before it confirms the order" instead: keep the synchronous call and add retries in the order service, because the caller has to [retry the invocation manually](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sync-error-caller-retries).
items.say: Lambda retries asynchronous events, so I'd invoke asynchronously and send failures to an SQS queue.

solvers.stem_only: Switch to asynchronous invocation (Lambda queues the event and retries on failure) and configure an on-failure destination such as an SQS queue to keep events that still fail.

items.stem: A company runs an AWS Lambda function that writes payment records to an Amazon RDS for MySQL database. The database runs in private subnets of a VPC. The VPC also has public subnets with a route to an internet gateway. The function must also call a payment provider's API on the internet. The function is not connected to the VPC yet. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way?
keywords: call a payment provider's API on the internet

options.text: Connect the function to the public subnets of the VPC, so that the function reaches the payment API through the internet gateway.
options.why: Connecting a function to a public subnet [doesn't give it internet access](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-public-subnet-no-internet) or a public IP address, so the call to the payment API fails.

options.text: Connect the function to private subnets whose route table sends internet-bound traffic to a NAT gateway in the VPC.
options.why: The function reaches the database [through the private subnets that contain the resources](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-attach-private-subnets), and those subnets [access the internet through the NAT gateway](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-public-subnet-no-internet).

options.text: Keep the function outside the VPC, and turn on public access for the database so that the function reaches both endpoints.
options.why: It works, because functions outside a VPC [have access to the public internet](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-attached-only-vpc-resources), but the database becomes reachable from the internet, which is less secure.

options.text: Connect the function to private subnets, and add a gateway VPC endpoint for the payment provider's API to their route table.
options.why: Gateway endpoints are [available only for AWS services including S3 and DynamoDB](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-faq-endpoint-types-gateway-interface), so no gateway endpoint reaches a payment provider.
options.misconception: believes that a gateway endpoint can reach any API outside the VPC

items.explanation: After you attach it, the function [can only access resources available within that VPC](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-attached-only-vpc-resources), so the internet path comes from the VPC. Private subnets keep the database private, and they [access the internet through the NAT gateway](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-public-subnet-no-internet). The database keeps its private address, and the function needs no public address.
items.takeaway: A VPC function reaches the internet from private subnets that [access the internet through the NAT gateway](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-public-subnet-no-internet), not from public subnets.
items.twin: If the stem said "must also read objects from an Amazon S3 bucket" instead: a gateway endpoint for Amazon S3, because gateway endpoints are [available only for AWS services including S3 and DynamoDB](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-faq-endpoint-types-gateway-interface).
items.say: Put the function in private subnets and send internet traffic through a NAT gateway; a public subnet gives it no internet.

solvers.stem_only: Attach the function to private subnets (with a security group allowed by the database) and route internet-bound traffic from those subnets through a NAT gateway in a public subnet; keep the database private.

items.stem: A company runs an AWS Lambda function that answers product search requests. At the start of every invocation, the handler downloads the same 300 MB reference file from an Amazon S3 bucket, which makes each request slow. The file changes once a week, and the company accepts that an execution environment keeps using an old copy for a few hours. The function serves a steady load of about 20 concurrent requests that does not grow. Every request must be fast, including the first request in each execution environment. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort? (Select TWO.)
keywords: the handler downloads the same 300 MB reference file
including the first request in each execution environment

options.text: Move the download out of the handler into the initialization code, so that the download runs once when Lambda prepares each environment.
options.why: Initialization code runs before the handler and [is not run again](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-static-init-reuse-connections) when an invocation uses a warm execution environment, so the download happens once per environment.

options.text: Store the reference file in an environment variable of the function, and read the variable at the start of each invocation.
options.why: All environment variables of a function together are limited to [4 KB](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-env-vars-size), which is far too small for the 300 MB file.
options.misconception: believes that environment variables can hold large data files

options.text: Cache the file in the /tmp directory from the handler, and download it again only when the file is not in /tmp yet.
options.why: The copy in /tmp [remains when the execution environment is frozen](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-tmp-transient-cache), but the first request in each environment still downloads the file.
options.misconception: believes that a cache that the handler fills also makes the first request in a new environment fast

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency of 20 on an alias of the function, and point the callers of the function at that alias.
options.why: Provisioned concurrency keeps [pre-initialized execution environments](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-pc-scales-beyond-setting), so the initialization code has run before the first request arrives.

options.text: Rebuild the search service as containers on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate, with tasks that load the file at startup and keep it in memory.
options.why: It works, but rebuilding the service on containers is far more development than one code change and one function setting.

items.explanation: The download repeats because it runs in the handler. Code outside the handler runs once per environment, because [Lambda can reuse the environment](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-warm-start-environment-reuse) for later requests. Provisioned concurrency runs that code before requests arrive, so the function [does not exhibit cold start behavior](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-pc-not-latest-no-cold-start). Lambda [terminates execution environments every few hours](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-environment-not-persistent), so a new copy arrives within hours of a change.
items.takeaway: Load a large shared file in initialization code, and add provisioned concurrency so that even the first request in an environment is fast.
items.twin: If the stem said "slow first requests in a new environment are acceptable" instead: the initialization code alone fits, because it [is not run again](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-static-init-reuse-connections) on a warm start.

solvers.stem_only: Move the S3 download from the handler into the initialization code (outside the handler) so it runs once per execution environment and is reused by later invocations; then configure provisioned concurrency (about 20) on an alias or version and point callers at it, so environments are initialized ahead of time and even the first request in each environment is fast. A /tmp cache inside the handler still makes the first request slow, and a rebuild on containers is more effort.

citations: docs/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-runtime-environment#The directory content remains when the e
docs/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-runtime-environment#The initialization code is not run again

items.stem: A company exposes one AWS Lambda function to about 40 partner companies over HTTPS. Each partner must use its own key, and the company must restrict each partner to an agreed number of requests per day. The security team requires AWS WAF rules in front of the endpoint to block common web attacks. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: an agreed number of requests per day

options.text: Create a function URL with the NONE auth type, and check each partner's key and daily request count in the function code.
options.why: With auth type NONE the URL is [public (no authentication)](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-furl-auth-public-or-iam), the key and quota checks become code, and AWS WAF stays missing.
options.misconception: builds API key and quota checks into the function code

options.text: Create a function URL with the AWS_IAM auth type, and attach a usage plan for each partner and an AWS WAF web ACL to the function URL.
options.why: [API keys for usage plans](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-apigw-extra-features-waf-keys) and [WAF integration for additional security](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-apigw-extra-features-waf-keys) are features that API Gateway adds and function URLs lack.

options.text: Put an Amazon API Gateway REST API in front of the function, with an API key and usage plan per partner and an AWS WAF web ACL.
options.why: API Gateway gives [API keys for usage plans](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-apigw-extra-features-waf-keys) and [WAF integration for additional security](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-apigw-extra-features-waf-keys), so each partner gets a key and a daily quota behind the WAF rules.

options.text: Create an Application Load Balancer with the function as a target, an AWS WAF web ACL, and a listener rule for each partner's key.
options.why: It can route requests and use AWS WAF, but a daily quota per partner becomes custom code, which API Gateway usage plans give without code.
options.misconception: expects a load balancer to count requests for each client

items.explanation: Three needs decide it: a key per partner, a daily quota per partner and AWS WAF. API Gateway is the better choice for [production applications at scale](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-apigw-better-for-production), and its usage plans and WAF integration cover all three. A function URL suits [simple applications or prototyping](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-furl-recommended-simple-apps).
items.takeaway: Per-client API keys, quotas and AWS WAF point to API Gateway, not to a Lambda function URL.
items.twin: If the stem said "one internal team calls the function, and no keys, quotas or AWS WAF rules are needed" instead: a function URL that can [require IAM authentication](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-furl-auth-public-or-iam), because it suits [simple applications or prototyping](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-furl-recommended-simple-apps).
items.say: Keys, quotas per partner and WAF are API Gateway features, so I'd put a REST API in front of the function.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: one function, HTTPS for partners, a key for each partner, a daily request limit for each partner, and AWS WAF rules in front of the endpoint.
Before I look at the options, I predict Amazon API Gateway, because API keys for usage plans and AWS WAF integration are features that API Gateway adds and function URLs lack.

I remove the function URL with auth type NONE, because the key and quota checks become my own code and AWS WAF is missing. I remove the function URL with IAM authentication, because usage plans and AWS WAF are not features of function URLs.

Between the REST API and the Application Load Balancer the difference is the daily quota; the stem says each partner gets an agreed number of requests per day, so usage plans decide it, and the load balancer would need custom code for the count.
Check: the REST API with an API key and a usage plan per partner and an AWS WAF web ACL meets every constraint without custom code. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Front the function with an API Gateway REST API: one API key per partner, usage plans with daily quotas, and an AWS WAF web ACL associated with the API stage.

citations: www/api-gateway/faqs#Usage plans help you declare plans for t

items.stem: A company runs a document-analysis service on AWS Lambda. A new version of the function needs machine learning libraries that are about 2 GB in size when unzipped. This is more than a .zip deployment package allows. The company wants to keep running the code as a Lambda function. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: about 2 GB in size when unzipped
keep running the code as a Lambda function

options.text: Build the function and its libraries into a container image, and create the function from that container image.
options.why: A function can deploy from [container images](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-deploy-zip-or-image), and an image can hold [10 GB](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-container-image-10-gb) uncompressed, enough for the libraries.

options.text: Split the libraries across five Lambda layers, so that each layer stays below the size quota of one deployment package.
options.why: Layers add no room: the function and all its layers together stay within the [250 MB](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-layers-five-and-250-mb) unzipped quota.

options.text: Push the container image to an Amazon ECR repository in the same AWS Region as the function.
options.why: A container image function uses an image from an Amazon ECR repository [in the same AWS Region](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-container-image-ecr-same-region) as the function.

options.text: Upload the .zip deployment package to an Amazon S3 bucket first, and create the function from the package in that bucket.
options.why: You [upload larger files with Amazon S3](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-zip-package-50-mb), but the unzipped contents stay limited to [250 MB](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-package-250-mb-unzipped).
options.misconception: believes that an upload through Amazon S3 raises the unzipped size quota

options.text: Install the libraries on an Amazon EC2 instance, and have the function forward each document to the instance for analysis.
options.why: It works, but the team runs and patches an instance and writes forwarding code, which a container image avoids.

items.explanation: The unzipped contents of a .zip package are limited to [250 MB](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-package-250-mb-unzipped), so the 2 GB of libraries need another format. Lambda also deploys [container images](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-deploy-zip-or-image), up to [10 GB](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-container-image-10-gb) in size. The image comes from Amazon ECR [in the same AWS Region](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-container-image-ecr-same-region) as the function.
items.takeaway: Dependencies larger than a .zip package allows go into a container image in Amazon ECR, in the function's own Region.
items.twin: If the stem said "about 100 MB in size when unzipped" instead: a .zip package or a layer still works, because the function and its layers can use [250 MB](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-layers-five-and-250-mb) unzipped.

solvers.stem_only: Package the function as a container image (much larger size limit than .zip plus layers), push the image to an ECR repository in the same Region, and create the function from the image.

items.stem: A media company receives video files in an Amazon S3 bucket at unpredictable times, sometimes several files in one minute and sometimes none for hours. Each new file must be converted to a smaller format for mobile users. Each file takes about 30 seconds to process. The company has a small operations team. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: Each file takes about 30 seconds to process

options.text: Configure an S3 event notification that invokes an AWS Lambda function for each new file, and convert the file inside the function before the function returns.
options.why: Amazon S3 invokes the function with an [event-driven; asynchronous invocation](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-trigger-s3-async) for each file, and a 30-second file fits in one invocation.

options.text: Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule for new S3 objects that runs an Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate for each file, and convert the file in the task.
options.why: It works, but a rule, a task definition and an image are more to run, and AWS suggests functions for [event-driven tasks, unpredictable workloads](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-choose-functions-event-driven-unpredictable).

options.text: Run Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum size of one, and have the instances check the bucket for new files every minute.
options.why: The team patches and scales the instances, and [polling can be highly inefficient](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-eda-polling-inefficient) when Amazon S3 can push an event for each file.
options.misconception: keeps instances running to poll for files that Amazon S3 can announce as events

options.text: Configure an S3 event notification that invokes an AWS Lambda function for each new file, and request a function timeout above 15 minutes in Service Quotas.
options.why: The timeout is a function configuration quota, and of those quotas AWS says [except as noted, they can't be changed](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-config-quotas-not-changeable).

items.explanation: The files arrive at unpredictable times, and each one needs seconds of work. AWS suggests functions for [event-driven tasks, unpredictable workloads](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-choose-functions-event-driven-unpredictable), and a standard invocation can run [up to 15 minutes](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-best-suited-short-invocations). An S3 event notification invokes the function for each file, so nothing runs between files, and the team manages no servers or tasks.
items.takeaway: Short, event-driven work that arrives at unpredictable times fits a Lambda function that an S3 event invokes.
items.twin: If the stem said "Each file is long-running: it takes about 40 minutes to process." instead: containers on AWS Fargate, because a function stops at [15 minutes per invocation](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-no-execution-time-limit).
items.say: Each file takes seconds and arrives at random times, so an S3 event invokes a Lambda function for each one.

solvers.stem_only: 30 seconds per file fits well within the Lambda timeout: S3 event notification invokes a Lambda function that converts each file.

items.stem: A company runs workloads on Amazon EC2 instances, on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate, and on AWS Lambda. The total compute usage is steady-state and will stay at about the same level for the next 3 years. During that time, the company plans to move some workloads between these three compute services. The company wants a commitment discount for this usage. Which purchase option is the MOST cost-effective?
keywords: move some workloads between these three compute services

options.text: Buy a three-year EC2 Instance Savings Plan, and apply its discount to the EC2, Fargate and Lambda usage.
options.why: [Compute Savings Plans](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sp-ec2-instance-plans-exclude-lambda) apply to Lambda usage, and EC2 Instance Savings Plans do not, so the Lambda part stays at On-Demand rates.

options.text: Buy three-year Standard Reserved Instances for the EC2 instances, and pay On-Demand rates for the Fargate and Lambda usage.
options.why: It works for the EC2 part, but the serverless work stays at On-Demand rates, because [Compute Savings Plans](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sp-ec2-instance-plans-exclude-lambda) are the plans that cover Lambda.

options.text: Buy a three-year Compute Savings Plan that commits to an hourly spend for the EC2, Fargate and Lambda usage together.
options.why: Compute Savings Plans apply to EC2 and [also cover Fargate and Lambda usage](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility), so the discount follows the work when it moves between services.

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency on every Lambda function, and pay On-Demand rates for the EC2 and Fargate usage.
options.why: Provisioned concurrency is no discount: [it increases costs](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-pc-costs-while-idle), because you pay for the provisioned instances even when they handle no requests.
options.misconception: takes provisioned concurrency for a commitment discount

items.explanation: The usage is steady for three years and moves between EC2, Fargate and Lambda. Compute Savings Plans apply [regardless of Region, instance family, operating system](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility) and [also cover Fargate and Lambda usage](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility), so one plan covers all the work wherever it runs.
items.takeaway: Mixed EC2, Fargate and Lambda usage that moves between services fits a Compute Savings Plan.
items.twin: If the stem said "all the usage runs on one EC2 instance family in one Region" instead: an EC2 Instance Savings Plan, because it applies to [a specific instance family within a Region](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility) for a higher discount.
items.say: For EC2, Fargate and Lambda together, a Compute Savings Plan covers all three.

solvers.stem_only: A Compute Savings Plan (three-year) covers EC2, Fargate and Lambda and stays flexible when workloads move between them.

items.stem: A company runs a public API on Amazon API Gateway. The API invokes several AWS Lambda functions in one AWS Region. During monthly sales campaigns, traffic has sudden spikes, and some API calls fail with TooManyRequestsException errors. Amazon CloudWatch metrics show that the total concurrent executions of all functions in the Region reach the account quota at those times. The company must ensure that all requests are served during the next campaign. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: the total concurrent executions of all functions in the Region reach the account quota
ensure that all requests are served

options.text: Move the API code to Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer that scales on request count.
options.why: It works, because instances have no Lambda concurrency quota, but the team then patches and scales servers, which is far more work than one quota request.

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency on every function for the campaign period, so that the functions get extra capacity above the account quota.
options.why: Provisioned concurrency adds no capacity: it [incurs charges to your AWS account](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-provisioned-concurrency-charges) and counts toward the same account limit.
options.misconception: believes that provisioned concurrency adds capacity above the account concurrency quota

options.text: Request an increase of the Lambda concurrent executions quota for the Region in Service Quotas, sized for the campaign peak with headroom.
options.why: All functions in the Region share the quota, and the default can be raised to [tens of thousands](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-concurrent-executions-default) through [Service Quotas](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-limit-increase-service-quotas).

options.text: Keep the current configuration, because Lambda scales every function on demand without a limit and the errors stop after the spikes.
options.why: Requests above the limit fail with a [throttling error (429 status code)](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-throttle-429), so the same errors return at the next campaign peak.

items.explanation: The metrics show the Region-wide total at the quota, so Lambda throttles the extra requests. The concurrent executions quota applies [per AWS Region](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-quota-scope-region-vs-vpc) to all functions together, and a request to raise it goes through [Service Quotas](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-limit-increase-service-quotas). One request before the campaign fixes the limit without a change to the API or the code.
items.takeaway: Throttling at the Region-wide concurrency quota is fixed with a Service Quotas increase, not with provisioned concurrency.
items.twin: If the stem said "one function reaches its reserved concurrency" instead: raise that function's reserved concurrency, because it is a cap that you set to [reserve a subset of your account concurrency limit](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control).
items.say: All functions in the Region share one concurrency quota, so I'd request an increase in Service Quotas before the campaign.

solvers.stem_only: The account-level Regional concurrency quota is the bottleneck; request a quota increase in Service Quotas sized for the peak.

items.stem: A company runs an order API on Amazon API Gateway. The API invokes an AWS Lambda function that writes each order to a small Amazon RDS for MySQL database. During traffic spikes, so many copies of the function connect at the same time that the database fails. The function must never run more than 50 copies at the same time. Clients must receive the result of each order in the API response, and the clients already retry any request that fails. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: The function must never run more than 50 copies at the same time
Clients must receive the result of each order in the API response

options.text: Set the reserved concurrency of the function to 50, and keep the API Gateway integration pointed at the function as it is today.
options.why: Reserved concurrency can [cap traffic rates to downstream resources](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control), so Lambda runs 50 copies or fewer and throttles the rest, which the clients retry.

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency of 50 on a published alias of the function, and point the API Gateway integration at that alias.
options.why: Provisioned concurrency is no ceiling, because Lambda can scale the function [above and beyond your provisioned concurrency setting](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-pc-scales-beyond-setting).

options.text: Place an Amazon SQS queue between API Gateway and the function, and set the maximum concurrency of the event source mapping to 50.
options.why: It limits the copies, but API Gateway answers when the message is in the queue, so clients no longer receive the order result in the API response.
options.misconception: believes that a queue in front of a function still returns the result of the function to the API caller

options.text: Move the code into containers on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Amazon ECS service that runs no more than 50 tasks.
options.why: It can hold the limit, but moving the whole API to containers is far more to build and run than one setting on the function.

items.explanation: The database fails because too many copies connect at once, so the fix is a ceiling on one function. AWS says to configure reserved concurrency to [limit how high your function can scale](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-bp-reserved-protects-downstream). Lambda throttles the requests above the ceiling, the clients retry them, and the setting [incurs no additional charges](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-reserved-concurrency-no-charge). The API stays synchronous, so each client still gets its order result.
items.takeaway: Reserved concurrency caps one function, and provisioned concurrency prepares environments without a cap.
items.twin: If the stem said "After quiet periods, the first requests take several seconds" instead: provisioned concurrency on an alias, because it keeps functions [ready to respond in double-digit milliseconds](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-snapstart-vs-pc-guide).
items.say: I'd set reserved concurrency to fifty, because it caps the function, so the database never sees more than fifty copies.

solvers.stem_only: Set reserved concurrency of 50 on the function. Reserved concurrency is also the maximum, so Lambda throttles invocations above 50 and API Gateway returns an error that the clients already retry; the integration stays synchronous so clients still get the order result. A queue would break the synchronous response, provisioned concurrency does not cap concurrency, and moving to containers adds overhead.

items.stem: A company stores customer uploads in an Amazon S3 bucket. Amazon S3 invokes an AWS Lambda function for each new object. Some uploads are malformed, and the function fails on every attempt to process them. Today, these failed events are retried and then lost. The operations team must keep a record of each failed event, with details about the failed invocation, as an object in a separate S3 bucket. The team must receive each record as soon as possible after the first failure. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
keywords: as an object in a separate S3 bucket
as soon as possible after the first failure

options.text: Configure an on-failure destination for asynchronous invocations of the function, and choose the separate S3 bucket as the destination.
options.why: Lambda can send records of asynchronous invocations to [An Amazon S3 bucket (on failure only)](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-async-destination-targets), as a record with details about the failed invocation.

options.text: Set the maximum retry attempts in the asynchronous invocation configuration of the function to 0, so that a failed event is not retried.
options.why: The retry count can be set [between 0 and 2](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-async-retry-attempts-0-to-2); at 0, the first failure goes to the destination at once.

options.text: Configure an Amazon SQS standard queue as the dead-letter queue of the function, and read the failed events from that queue.
options.why: A dead-letter queue can be an [Amazon SQS queue or an Amazon SNS topic](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-dlq-sqs-or-sns), so no record reaches the S3 bucket.

options.text: Configure an on-failure destination for asynchronous invocations of the function, and choose an Amazon SNS FIFO topic as the destination.
options.why: A FIFO topic is an [unsupported destination type](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-destination-fifo-unsupported) for asynchronous invocation records, so no record arrives.
options.misconception: believes that any Amazon SNS topic can receive invocation records

options.text: Add error handling code to the function that writes each failed event and its error message as an object to the separate S3 bucket.
options.why: It works, but custom error code in the function is more to build and maintain than two settings in the asynchronous invocation configuration.

items.explanation: Amazon S3 invokes the function asynchronously. After a failure, Lambda tries [two more times](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-async-default-two-retries), and then [Lambda discards it](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-async-discard-then-destination) unless a destination keeps it. An on-failure destination can be an S3 bucket, which receives a record with details about the invocation, and a retry count of 0 sends the record after the first failure.
items.takeaway: Failed asynchronous events go to an on-failure destination, which can be an S3 bucket; 0 retries sends them at once.
items.twin: If the stem said "must keep each failed event in an Amazon SQS queue" instead: a dead-letter queue also fits, because it can be an [Amazon SQS queue or an Amazon SNS topic](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-dlq-sqs-or-sns).
items.say: An on-failure destination writes each failed event with its invocation details to the S3 bucket, and zero retries sends it right after the first failure.

solvers.stem_only: S3 invokes the function asynchronously. Configure an on-failure destination for asynchronous invocation with the separate S3 bucket as the destination: Lambda writes an invocation record with the event and details about the failed invocation (error, request context). To get the record right after the first failure, set the maximum retry attempts of the asynchronous invocation configuration to 0. A dead-letter queue keeps only the event with few details and is a queue, not an S3 object; custom error-handling code is more overhead and misses timeouts.

solvers.flag: A second pair, A and B (retries off, plus code in the function that writes the failed event to the S3 bucket at the first failure), is defensible because the stem does not say that failures include timeouts or runtime crashes that the function code cannot catch, so B is not clearly excluded and only the phrase 'details about the failed invocation' plus 'least operational overhead' separates it from E.

items.stem: A media company receives video files in an Amazon S3 bucket at unpredictable times, sometimes several files in one minute and sometimes none for hours. Each new file must be converted to a smaller format for mobile users. Each file is long-running: it takes about 40 minutes to process. The company has a small operations team. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: it takes about 40 minutes to process

options.text: Configure an S3 event notification that invokes an AWS Lambda function for each new file, and convert the file inside the function before the function returns.
options.why: A function stops at [15 minutes per invocation](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-no-execution-time-limit), so every 40-minute file times out, however the event arrives.

options.text: Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule for new S3 objects that runs an Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate for each file, and convert the file in the task.
options.why: Fargate has [no hard limit on execution time](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-no-execution-time-limit), and you [run containers without having to manage servers](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-guide-fargate-no-servers-for-containers), one task for each file.

options.text: Run Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group with a minimum size of one, and have the instances check the bucket for new files every minute.
options.why: It works for long files, but the team patches and scales instances that run between files, which is more work than one task for each file.

options.text: Configure an S3 event notification that invokes an AWS Lambda function for each new file, and request a function timeout above 15 minutes in Service Quotas.
options.why: The timeout is a function configuration quota, and of those quotas AWS says [except as noted, they can't be changed](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-config-quotas-not-changeable).

items.explanation: A 40-minute job does not fit in a function, because the maximum timeout is [900 seconds](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-timeout-max). AWS positions Fargate for [long-running applications, microservices, or batch processing](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-fargate-long-running-lambda-short). An EventBridge rule starts one task for each new file, and the task stops when its file is done, so nothing runs between files.
items.takeaway: A job longer than the function timeout runs as a container task on AWS Fargate, not in a Lambda function.
items.twin: If the stem said "Each file takes about 30 seconds to process." instead: an S3 event notification and a Lambda function, because AWS suggests functions for [event-driven tasks, unpredictable workloads](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-choose-functions-event-driven-unpredictable).
items.say: Forty minutes is more than a function can run, so each file starts a Fargate task instead.

solvers.stem_only: 40 minutes exceeds the Lambda maximum timeout of 15 minutes; use an event-driven container task, for example EventBridge rule on S3 object created that runs an ECS task on Fargate per file.

items.stem: A company uses an Amazon SQS standard queue to decouple an order service from an AWS Lambda function. An event source mapping invokes the function with batches of messages. A few malformed messages make the function fail on every attempt. These messages return to the queue again and again and fill the function logs with errors. The company wants to keep the malformed messages for later analysis and stop the repeated processing. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: An event source mapping invokes the function
keep the malformed messages for later analysis

options.text: Add code to the function that copies each malformed message to an Amazon S3 bucket and then deletes the message from the queue.
options.why: It works, but parsing, copying and deleting code is more to build and maintain than one redrive policy on the queue.

options.text: Configure a dead-letter queue on the function, so that Lambda sends each message that fails every attempt to a second SQS queue.
options.why: A function's [dead letter queue](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-dlq-after-retries) serves asynchronous invocations; for an SQS source, the redrive policy of the source queue decides where failed messages go.

options.text: Set the visibility timeout of the source queue lower than the function timeout, so that failed messages return to the queue sooner.
options.why: It is a misconfiguration: the function timeout [must be less than or equal to](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sqs-timeout-not-above-visibility) the visibility timeout, so messages reappear while a batch still runs, and it keeps no message.
options.misconception: believes that a shorter visibility timeout clears messages that keep failing

options.text: Configure a redrive policy on the source queue that moves a message to an SQS dead-letter queue after a maxReceiveCount of 5.
options.why: For a queue source, the [visibility timeout and redrive policy](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-queue-esm-retry-set-on-queue) decide where failed messages go, and AWS suggests a maxReceiveCount of [at least 5](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sqs-dlq-maxreceivecount-5).

items.explanation: With an SQS event source mapping, a failed message becomes visible again and is retried. The [visibility timeout and redrive policy](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-queue-esm-retry-set-on-queue) of the source queue decide the retries and where failed messages go. A redrive policy moves a message that keeps failing to a dead-letter queue, where it waits for analysis.
items.takeaway: For an SQS event source, failed messages reach a dead-letter queue through the redrive policy of the source queue.
items.twin: If the stem said "an Amazon Kinesis data stream" instead: an on-failure destination on the event source mapping, because it sends discarded records to an [Amazon SQS queue or Amazon SNS topic](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-kinesis-failure-destination-sqs-sns).
items.say: For an SQS source, the queue's own redrive policy moves the bad messages to a dead-letter queue.

solvers.stem_only: For an SQS event source, configure a redrive policy with a dead-letter queue on the source SQS queue (maxReceiveCount), not a Lambda DLQ.

items.stem: A company runs an order API on Amazon API Gateway with AWS Lambda functions. The functions write orders to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. Each copy of a function opens its own database connection. During traffic spikes, the database returns too many connections errors, and some orders fail. Every request must be served, and the solution must require minimal code changes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Set the reserved concurrency of the functions to 10, so that no more than 10 copies of the functions connect to the database at the same time.
options.why: Requests above the cap fail with a [throttling error (429 status code)](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-throttle-429), so orders still fail, and the stem says every request must be served.
options.misconception: caps the copies of the function when every request must still be served

options.text: Create an Amazon RDS Proxy for the DB instance, and change the database endpoint in the configuration of the functions to the proxy endpoint.
options.why: The proxy keeps a pool of connections that many function copies share, and Lambda functions benefit from the [connection pooling offered by RDS Proxy](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling).

options.text: Change the functions so that each invocation opens a new database connection at its start and closes the connection before it returns.
options.why: A connection for each invocation adds work, and many concurrent copies can still [exhaust database connection limits](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-db-connections-rds-proxy).

options.text: Move the database to a larger DB instance class that accepts more connections, and keep the functions and their connection code as they are.
options.why: A resize costs more and needs planning, and with fixed capacity [you might exceed your connection quota](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-rds-connection-quota-spikes) again at a larger spike.
options.misconception: believes that a larger database ends the connection problem, although connections still grow with concurrency

items.explanation: Each concurrent environment keeps its own connection, so high concurrency can [exhaust database connection limits](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-db-connections-rds-proxy). RDS Proxy lets applications [pool and share database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-definition-pool-share), and most applications can use it with [no code changes](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-faq-no-code-changes): the functions read a new endpoint. The proxy sits in the [same virtual private cloud (VPC) as the database](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-same-vpc-not-public), so functions that are not yet attached to that VPC also need that attachment.
items.takeaway: Many Lambda copies that exhaust database connections need RDS Proxy in front of the database.
items.twin: If the stem said "Some requests can be rejected during spikes to protect the database" instead: reserved concurrency also fits, because it can [cap traffic rates to downstream resources](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control).
items.say: RDS Proxy pools the connections, so every copy of the function shares a few database connections.

steps: I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead.
I mark the constraints: too many connections errors during spikes, every request must be served, and minimal code changes.
Before I look at the options, I predict reserved concurrency, because a cap on the copies of the function also caps the database connections.

I remove the connection for each invocation, because many concurrent copies still exhaust the connection limit. I remove the larger instance class, because the database keeps a fixed capacity and the resize costs more.

Between reserved concurrency and RDS Proxy the difference is what happens to the requests above the cap. My first idea breaks because Lambda answers those requests with a throttling error, and the stem says every request must be served. The proxy pools the connections instead, so every request still reaches the database.
Check: RDS Proxy serves every request, needs a new endpoint but no new code logic, and adds no servers to manage. Time: 90 seconds.

solvers.stem_only: Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance to pool and share connections; point the functions at the proxy endpoint.

items.stem: A company runs an order API on Amazon API Gateway. The API invokes an AWS Lambda function that writes each order to a small Amazon RDS for MySQL database. After quiet periods, the first requests take several seconds because new execution environments start. Traffic never needs more than 50 copies of the function, and the API must respond with low latency to every request. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: the first requests take several seconds
respond with low latency to every request

options.text: Set the reserved concurrency of the function to 50, and keep the API Gateway integration pointed at the function as it is today.
options.why: Reserved concurrency is a cap that you set to [reserve a subset of your account concurrency limit](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control), and it prepares no environment before a request arrives.

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency of 50 on a published alias of the function, and point the API Gateway integration at that alias.
options.why: Provisioned concurrency keeps functions [ready to respond in double-digit milliseconds](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-snapstart-vs-pc-guide), and API Gateway uses those environments because it invokes the alias.

options.text: Place an Amazon SQS queue between API Gateway and the function, and set the maximum concurrency of the event source mapping to 50.
options.why: A queue starts no environment ahead of time, so the first messages after a quiet period still wait for new environments, and the API stops returning results.
options.misconception: believes that a queue in front of a function removes the start-up delay of new environments

options.text: Move the code into containers on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Amazon ECS service whose tasks keep running between requests.
options.why: It works, because the tasks are already running when requests arrive, but moving the API to containers is far more work than one setting on an alias.

items.explanation: The slow first requests are cold starts: Lambda [downloads your code, starts the environment](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-cold-start-definition) before the handler runs. With provisioned concurrency, the function [does not exhibit cold start behavior](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-pc-not-latest-no-cold-start). API Gateway invokes the alias, so it [points to the correct function alias or version](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-pc-event-source-alias).
items.takeaway: Cold starts on a synchronous API go away with provisioned concurrency on the alias that the caller invokes.
items.twin: If the stem said "The function must never run more than 50 copies at the same time" instead: reserved concurrency of 50, because it can [cap traffic rates to downstream resources](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control).
items.say: Provisioned concurrency keeps fifty environments initialized on the alias, so no request waits for a cold start.

solvers.stem_only: Configure provisioned concurrency (50) on a published version or alias and have API Gateway invoke that alias, so environments are pre-initialized.

items.stem: A company runs a latency-sensitive API on Amazon API Gateway with an AWS Lambda function. To remove cold starts, a developer published a version of the function, created an alias named live that points to the version, and configured provisioned concurrency on the alias. However, users still see slow responses after quiet periods. The API Gateway integration invokes the function by its unqualified ARN. The API must respond with low latency. Which change will fix the problem with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: configured provisioned concurrency on the alias
invokes the function by its unqualified ARN

options.text: Configure reserved concurrency on the function equal to the provisioned concurrency, so that the function keeps its environments warm.
options.why: Reserved concurrency is a cap that you set to [reserve a subset of your account concurrency limit](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control); it prepares no environment, so the cold starts stay.

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency on the $LATEST version of the function, so that calls to the unqualified ARN use initialized environments.
options.why: Provisioned concurrency applies to a published version or an alias, [not the $LATEST version](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-pc-not-latest-no-cold-start).

options.text: Update the API Gateway integration so that it invokes the live alias of the function instead of the unqualified function ARN.
options.why: Provisioned environments serve a caller that [points to the correct function alias or version](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-pc-event-source-alias), so the integration has to invoke the live alias.

options.text: Move the API code to Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, with instances that keep running.
options.why: It works, because running instances need no start-up for each request, but moving the API to servers is far more work than changing one integration setting.

items.explanation: The provisioned environments belong to the live alias. If a function has an event source, the source has to call the alias or version that has them, or the function [won't use provisioned concurrency environments](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-pc-event-source-alias). The unqualified ARN does not use the alias, so requests still get new environments. Pointing the integration at live fixes this with one change.
items.takeaway: Provisioned concurrency helps callers that invoke its version or alias; an unqualified ARN gets new environments.
items.twin: If the stem said "configured reserved concurrency on the function" instead: configure provisioned concurrency on an alias, because provisioned concurrency gives [pre-initialized execution environments](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-pc-scales-beyond-setting).
items.say: The warm environments sit on the alias, so API Gateway has to call the alias, not the plain function name.

solvers.stem_only: Provisioned concurrency applies only to the qualified alias or version; point the API Gateway integration at the live alias ARN.

items.stem: A company runs a containerized web API for a mobile app on AWS Lambda. The API now receives a high, steady-state volume of requests all day, every day. Each request runs for about 1 second at a large memory setting, and the monthly Lambda bill grows with the request volume. The company wants to avoid managing servers. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?
keywords: a high, steady-state volume of requests all day, every day

options.text: Keep the API on Lambda, and buy an EC2 Instance Savings Plan that matches the hourly compute spend of the function.
options.why: The plan leaves the Lambda bill as it is, because [Compute Savings Plans](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-sp-ec2-instance-plans-exclude-lambda) apply to Lambda usage and EC2 Instance Savings Plans do not.

options.text: Keep the API on Lambda, and configure reserved concurrency for the function at the level of the daily peak so that no request is throttled.
options.why: It keeps the API working at the same price, because reserved concurrency [incurs no additional charges](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-reserved-concurrency-no-charge) and lowers no request or duration charge.

options.text: Run the API on Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer, and buy Reserved Instances for the instances.
options.why: The company then manages servers, which it wants to avoid, and a lower price does not save an option that misses a stated requirement.

options.text: Run the API as containers on AWS Fargate behind an Application Load Balancer, with an Amazon ECS service that scales on request load.
options.why: Fargate billing suits [sustained, high-throughput workloads](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vs-fargate-cost-by-volume), and you [run containers without having to manage servers](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-guide-fargate-no-servers-for-containers).

items.explanation: The decision guide says that you typically [pay less with Lambda at lower traffic volumes](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vs-fargate-cost-by-volume), while Fargate tends to cost less for [sustained, high-throughput workloads](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vs-fargate-cost-by-volume). The API is already a container, so it moves to an ECS service on Fargate, and the company still manages no servers.
items.takeaway: A high, steady request volume all day tends to cost less on AWS Fargate than on Lambda.
items.twin: If the stem said "receives a few thousand requests at unpredictable times each day" instead: stay on Lambda, because you typically [pay less with Lambda at lower traffic volumes](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vs-fargate-cost-by-volume).
items.say: At a high, steady load all day, Fargate usually costs less than Lambda, and there are still no servers to manage.

solvers.stem_only: For high steady-state traffic, run the container on ECS with Fargate behind an ALB: no servers to manage and cheaper than per-request Lambda billing at constant high load.

items.stem: A company processes clickstream records from an Amazon Kinesis data stream with an AWS Lambda function. The event source mapping uses the default settings. However, one malformed record makes the function fail, and processing of that record's shard stops for days while the other shards continue. The company wants to keep the full content of each failed record for later analysis and keep each shard moving. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: The event source mapping uses the default settings
keep the full content of each failed record

options.text: Configure a dead-letter queue on the function, so that Lambda moves the malformed record to an Amazon SQS queue after its retries end.
options.why: A function's [dead letter queue](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-dlq-after-retries) receives asynchronous events after their retries; a stream mapping keeps failed records in its own on-failure destination.

options.text: On the event source mapping, turn on bisect batch on function error, set a retry limit, and add an Amazon S3 bucket as the on-failure destination.
options.why: [BisectBatchOnFunctionError](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-stream-bisect-batch-on-error) isolates the bad record, the retry limit ends the loop, and an [Amazon S3 bucket](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-kinesis-on-failure-destination-targets) destination receives the entire invocation record.

options.text: Raise the parallelization factor of the event source mapping, so that other concurrent batches from the same shard move past the malformed record.
options.why: More batches for each shard keep no copy of the failed record, and Lambda [stops processing additional records in a shard](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-kinesis-in-order-stops-on-error) after an error.
options.misconception: believes that more concurrent batches for each shard skip a record that keeps failing

options.text: Add code to the function that catches parse errors, writes each malformed record to an Amazon S3 bucket, and returns success for the batch.
options.why: It works, but parsing and copying code in the function is more to build and maintain than three settings on the event source mapping.

items.explanation: With the default settings, [failed records are retried until the record expires](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-kinesis-max-retry-attempts), so a bad record can block its shard for [up to one week](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-kinesis-bad-record-block-one-week). Bisect batch isolates the record, a retry limit stops the loop, and an S3 on-failure destination keeps the whole invocation record while the shard moves on.
items.takeaway: A poison record in a stream needs bisect batch, a retry limit and an on-failure destination on the mapping.
items.twin: If the stem said "an Amazon SQS standard queue" instead: a redrive policy on the source queue, because the [visibility timeout and redrive policy](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-queue-esm-retry-set-on-queue) decide where failed messages go.
items.say: Split the failed batch, cap the retries and send the bad record to an S3 on-failure destination, so the shard keeps moving.

solvers.stem_only: On the Kinesis event source mapping, turn on bisect batch on function error and set a maximum retry attempts (and/or maximum record age) so a failing batch is eventually skipped and the shard keeps moving; add an on-failure destination that keeps the full record content, which is an Amazon S3 bucket (SQS or SNS destinations receive only metadata about the batch, not the records). A function dead-letter queue applies only to asynchronous invocations, not stream event source mappings.

solvers.flag: Option B (catch parse errors in the function code, write the record to S3, return success) also keeps the full record and keeps the shard moving; only the 'least operational overhead' phrase separates it from C (configuration only versus custom code), which is a weak discriminator.
citations: docs/lambda/latest/dg/with-kinesis#When you increase the number of concurre

solvers.flag: Option C is also defensible: the Lambda documentation says the on-failure record for a stream source does not include the actual records (only batch metadata, to be used to read them back from the stream), so A may not 'keep the full content of each failed record' as the stem demands, while C stores the full record in S3 and returns success.

items.stem: A company runs an order workflow as a chain of five AWS Lambda functions. Each function calls the next function synchronously with the AWS SDK and waits for its answer. Retry logic is written by hand in every function. Costs are higher than expected, and when an order fails, the team cannot see which step failed. The company wants to orchestrate the steps with managed retries and a clear view of each step. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: orchestrate the steps with managed retries

options.text: Merge the five functions into one larger function that runs every step in order, and keep the retry code for each step inside it.
options.why: The hand-written retries stay, and one large function makes it [hard to enforce least privilege](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-monolith-breaks-least-privilege), because its role allows every resource.
options.misconception: believes that one large function is simpler to run than a managed workflow

options.text: Raise the timeout of each calling function, so that each caller waits longer for the next function and has time for its retries.
options.why: Longer timeouts keep the callers [running in a wait state](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-chaining-cost-wait-state), and [you pay for the duration of an invocation](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-chaining-cost-wait-state).
options.misconception: believes that a longer wait fixes a chain of synchronous calls

options.text: Create an AWS Step Functions state machine that runs each function as one task, with retry and error handling rules for each step.
options.why: Step Functions gives [visual workflow orchestration](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-step-functions-orchestrate-errors), runs one function for each task and [handles errors at each step](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-step-functions-orchestrate-errors).

options.text: Put an Amazon SQS queue between each pair of functions, and build a dashboard from custom metrics that each function publishes about its step.
options.why: It works, because AWS suggests to [use an Amazon SQS queue between Lambda functions](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-chaining-anti-pattern-sqs-or-step-functions), but queues and a custom dashboard are more to build.

items.explanation: Functions that call other functions directly are [generally an anti-pattern](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-chaining-anti-pattern-sqs-or-step-functions), because each caller waits and is billed while it waits. Step Functions coordinates the flow between the functions and [handles errors at each step](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-step-functions-orchestrate-errors), so retries leave the code and each step is visible in the workflow.
items.takeaway: A chain of functions that call each other synchronously becomes a Step Functions workflow.
items.twin: If the stem said "each step hands off work, and nobody needs a view of the flow" instead: queues between the functions fit, because AWS suggests to [use an Amazon SQS queue between Lambda functions](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-chaining-anti-pattern-sqs-or-step-functions).
items.say: Functions that call functions and wait pay twice, so I'd move the chain into a Step Functions workflow.

solvers.stem_only: Orchestrate with an AWS Step Functions state machine: each Lambda function is a task with Retry and Catch rules, and the execution history shows each step.

items.stem: A company runs many AWS Lambda functions in one AWS Region. Each night, a batch job invokes thousands of copies of one function at the same time and uses all of the concurrency that the account has in the Region. During the batch job, the mission-critical payment function is throttled. The company must ensure that the payment function can always scale to its usual peak of 200 concurrent executions. What should a solutions architect do?
keywords: uses all of the concurrency that the account has in the Region
the mission-critical payment function is throttled

options.text: Increase the memory setting of the payment function.
options.why: Memory changes CPU, because Lambda allocates CPU [in proportion to the amount of memory](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-cpu-proportional-to-memory), and it adds no concurrency to the payment function.
options.misconception: believes that a larger memory setting reserves capacity for a function

options.text: Change nothing, because each function scales on demand without a limit.
options.why: All functions share the Regional pool, and requests above it fail with a [throttling error (429 status code)](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-throttle-429), as the payment function shows.

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency for the batch function.
options.why: Provisioned concurrency sets no ceiling, because the batch function can scale [above and beyond your provisioned concurrency setting](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-pc-scales-beyond-setting).

options.text: Configure reserved concurrency of 200 for the payment function.
options.why: Reserved concurrency can [reserve a subset of your account concurrency limit](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control) for one function, so the batch job leaves those 200 units free.

items.explanation: All functions in the Region draw from one pool, so the batch job can use it up. Reserved concurrency sets aside part of the pool for the payment function, and the setting [incurs no additional charges](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-reserved-concurrency-no-charge). It also caps the payment function at 200, which matches its usual peak.
items.takeaway: To keep capacity for a critical function, give that function reserved concurrency.
items.twin: If the stem said "the batch job overloads a downstream database" instead: set reserved concurrency on the batch function, because it can [cap traffic rates to downstream resources](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-per-function-concurrency-control).
items.say: Reserved concurrency sets aside two hundred for the payment function, so the batch job cannot take them.

solvers.stem_only: Set reserved concurrency of 200 on the payment function so that this concurrency is set aside and other functions cannot use it.
